checkpoints: The problem: a session living in local RAM pins each user to the exact node holding it, forcing a sticky session.
Consequence #1: when that node dies, or the LB round-robins the user onto a different node, they are logged out immediately.
Consequence #2: sticky-session pinning also defeats the goal of spreading load evenly across nodes.
The contract: a small shared session-store with get(sessionId), set(sessionId, session, ttl), and delete(sessionId), backed by one central in-memory store like Redis instead of per-process RAM.
Pushing state out like this makes the service stateless: any node can serve any request, so round-robin (or Least Connections when load is uneven) becomes valid.
This statelessness is the precondition for scaling out — without it, adding nodes just adds more places for a user to get logged out rather than adding up capacity.
The trade-off: every session read/write now costs one extra network hop to the store, in exchange for near-unbounded scale-out and no session loss when a node dies.
The caveat: the central store is now shared, critical infrastructure — if it isn't highly available on its own (replication/cluster), the SPOF has just moved into the store, not been removed.

The root cause: a single ping with a 1-strike policy carries no memory, so it can't distinguish a transient GC pause or load spike from a real crash — it evicts immediately and readmits immediately on the very next successful ping.

Flapping is actively harmful, not just noisy: every eviction reroutes the node's in-flight connections onto the remaining nodes, spiking their load right as the recovering node is about to rejoin and take load back.
The design gives each node a state machine — HEALTHY, SUSPECT (recent failures, still in the pool), and UNHEALTHY (evicted) — instead of a bare boolean.
The load balancer pings every node on a fixed interval, e.g. 2-5 seconds, frequent enough to notice real failures quickly but sparse enough not to be a load source itself.
A node moves HEALTHY → SUSPECT → UNHEALTHY only after an unhealthy threshold of consecutive failures (e.g. 3 in a row), so a single blip no longer evicts anything.

Getting back in is stricter: a healthy threshold of consecutive successes (e.g. 2) is required before UNHEALTHY → HEALTHY, so a node must demonstrate real recovered stability rather than answer one lucky ping.

The trade-off: raising the unhealthy threshold buys strong immunity to noise, but a truly dead node now survives up to threshold × interval seconds longer inside the pool (e.g. up to 6 seconds at 3 failures / 2-second interval) before eviction.

For a node that keeps hovering right at the threshold and repeatedly flaps over the long run, a fixed threshold isn't enough — that calls for a phi-accrual failure detector (confidence scored from recent response timing) or exponential backoff that makes a re-flapping node earn its way back more slowly.
The average is dominated by the fast majority: if 99% of requests finish in 15-30ms and 1% take several seconds, the mean still comes out as a small, clean number, hiding the suffering minority.
Percentiles expose the blind spot: P99 is the experience of the slowest 1% of requests and P95 is the slowest 5%, matching the users who actually file complaints — a group the average never isolates.
At the scale of millions of users, the hidden tail is not a rounding error: 1% of a few million users is tens of thousands of real people having a bad experience every single day.
Conclusion: P95/P99 must be measured and alerted on instead of the average, since only percentiles reflect the real user experience while a mean creates a false sense of safety.
The slow tail is usually not random — it typically points to a concrete, investigable and fixable cause, such as a GC pause or a temporarily overloaded node, not "bad luck" to accept.
When the cable is cut, the node is blind: it cannot tell whether the peer crashed or the network was merely severed, so it has to decide immediately, without waiting to see through the cut.
On the Internet, a partition (P) is a given — cable cuts, packet loss, GC pauses happen sooner or later — so the real choice an architect makes is C or A on top of it.
Pure CA only exists on a single machine that has no network to cut in the first place.
CP means syncing the peer before committing: if the peer is unreachable, the node aborts and returns an error — availability is sacrificed, but no balance ever diverges.

AP means committing locally first and syncing in the background: the write always succeeds, but the two regions now hold different balances until the link comes back and the background sync converges them — that's eventual consistency, "they will become the same", not "the same right now".
For a bank I'd pick CP: refusing a transfer for a while is far better than allowing a double-spend because two regions silently disagree on the balance.
Something like Facebook likes or a shopping cart, on the other hand, would pick AP — that data tolerates temporary divergence, and staying responsive matters more than a momentary mismatch.
Jumping straight to "Kafka + Redis + microservices" with no load numbers is over-engineering — a sledgehammer for a nut.
The point of estimation is to quantify the problem so the architecture follows the data, not personal preference: writeQps, readQps, peakQps, and 10-year storage form a decision function.

One single number is enough to flip the conclusion — cross the peak-QPS threshold and the recommendation goes from "one relational DB with read replicas is enough" to "a distributed store plus a cache is required"; below that threshold, reaching for a distributed store is wasted resources and unnecessary operational complexity.

Step order matters because the steps depend on each other: clarification pins the assumptions (read/write ratio, target load, latency budget) that estimation consumes as input, so estimating before clarifying means inventing your own inputs and getting the architecture wrong at the root.
The estimate is deliberately coarse — good enough to decide fast, not meant to be exact.
The whole process is a loop: a constraint discovered later (say, at the deep-dive step) sends you back to revise the numbers and the architecture at an earlier step.

Each replica adds its own CPU/throughput straight into the total, so at first glance scaling looks like it stays linear forever — but that only holds while the load is divisible and nothing shared sits behind the replicas.

The moment there is a shared resource that does not scale with the node count — a single database, a distributed lock, a central queue — adding nodes stops helping: the new replicas just pile more contention onto that one point.
This is Amdahl's law in practice: the shared/serial fraction caps the achievable speedup, so throughput saturates instead of continuing to climb.
To keep scaling you must attack the contention itself — shard the database, add read replicas for a read-heavy load, or remove the distributed lock/central queue — not add more app nodes.

None of this even applies unless the service is stateless in the first place: if replicas still hold local session state, requests can't be freely distributed and the additive mechanism breaks down before you ever reach the database bottleneck.

CAP only speaks to the exact moment of a partition; PACELC completes it with the Else clause: when the network is healthy, you are still choosing between low Latency and strong Consistency — waiting for more replicas to agree costs latency.
So the trade-off is constant, not a failure-time-only event: a store can be PA/EL (available under partition, latency-leaning otherwise) or PC/EC (always favoring consistency).

Quorum makes this dialable: with N replicas, if writes wait for W acks and reads query R nodes, then W + R > N guarantees the write set and read set overlap in at least one node, and that overlapping node holds the latest write, so the read is guaranteed to see it.
If W + R ≤ N the two sets can be entirely disjoint, and a read may land on a node that hasn't updated yet and return stale data.

That's why an operations team can tune W and R per operation to slide between consistency and latency/availability without ever touching the database engine underneath — exactly the CAP trade-off, exposed as a knob rather than baked into a fixed architecture.

A per-instance field like `requestCount` lives in that one process's memory, so each of the N replicas behind the load balancer maintains its own independent counter that is never shared with or aggregated across the others.

A load balancer such as Nginx round-robins each incoming poll to an arbitrary replica, so two consecutive requests to the same public metrics URL can land on two completely different instances rather than sampling the same source twice.

Plotting consecutive polls as one continuous 'total cluster traffic' line is misleading when each point actually comes from a different replica with its own history — one poll might hit a replica that has served 120 requests over 300 seconds, and the next might hit a replica that just restarted with 4 requests and 20 seconds of uptime, producing a graph that looks like traffic randomly collapsed even though nothing was lost.

The `StatusService` code itself is correct: keeping request count, uptime, and memory usage as per-instance state is the expected, deliberate design for a stateless, horizontally-scalable service, since no state needs to be shared across containers for the service to function.

The actual defect is in the reader's assumption inside `ops-dashboard.ts` — it treats a single per-instance number reached through the load balancer as if it represented the whole cluster's traffic, when no global counter exists anywhere in the system.

Getting a real cluster-wide total requires bypassing the load balancer and scraping every replica directly — for example using Prometheus service discovery to hit each container's own metrics endpoint (such as `:3000/api/metrics`) individually — and then summing the per-instance values at the observability layer instead of trusting one round-robined read.

Labeling each scraped metric by its source instance (such as `servedBy`) preserves the ability to see each node's own trend separately in a tool like Grafana, in addition to the summed cluster-wide figure.

A correct fix can be verified by scraping all replicas directly at the same time and confirming the summed total stays stable and tracks real offered load, while any single replica's count sits at roughly one over N of that total.
Nginx's default load-balancing algorithm is round-robin, which picks the next backend purely by turn in the rotation and has no visibility into whether that node is currently busy or idle.

Because round-robin carries no notion of current load, a replica that is already stuck processing a heavy request still receives its next turn in the rotation, so new requests keep piling onto an already-blocked node instead of being routed elsewhere.

Node.js handles requests through a single event loop per process, so a CPU-bound synchronous handler like the heavy calculation occupies that event loop for its entire duration, and no other request on that replica — including a near-instant endpoint like /api/status — can be processed until it finishes.

This turns one replica into a hot node: its queue and latency balloon under a burst of heavy calls while the other replicas, which never receive a disproportionate share of blocking work, sit comparatively idle.
The underlying problem is an algorithm-to-workload mismatch — round-robin assumes uniform, low-variance requests — rather than a logic bug inside either the heavy or the status handler.

Switching the load-balancing method to least_conn routes each new request to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections, so a node stuck on a long-running request naturally receives fewer new requests instead of being fed more by blind rotation.

Offloading the CPU-bound work to a worker_threads pool keeps the main event loop free, so the replica can keep serving light requests like /api/status concurrently with the heavy computation instead of blocking on it.

The fix can be verified by sending a mixed load of heavy and light requests through the load balancer and confirming that latency spreads evenly across all replicas and no single node's queue grows unbounded afterward.

Fire-and-forget replication with only a logged warning on failure means an unreachable peer's write is never retried or redelivered, so the two regions diverge permanently instead of eventually converging.

"Eventual consistency" requires an actual mechanism to force divergent replicas back into agreement — durable redelivery such as an outbox or retry queue, plus a background anti-entropy loop — and a bare `.catch` that only logs provides neither.

When both regions accept writes to the same account during a network partition, reconnecting surfaces two different balance values with nothing in the code deciding which one wins; that is a missing conflict-resolution strategy, not a logging gap.

Resolving concurrent writes needs write metadata — a version number or vector clock — to detect that a conflict happened, plus an explicit merge rule such as last-write-wins or a CRDT to resolve it deterministically.
Applying naive last-write-wins to a money balance can silently lose or double-count funds, because the losing write is simply discarded rather than merged or reconciled.

Choosing AP for a money balance should be an explicit, questioned trade-off rather than a default; alternatives like a CP design or a quorum where W + R > N can preserve some availability without giving up correctness on financial data.

A senior-level review separates a genuine blocker — data loss from unretried writes plus absent conflict resolution — from minor nitpicks, and asks whether temporary divergence was ever an accepted trade-off for this kind of data.

Correctness for this design is verified with a partition test: write on both sides while disconnected, reconnect, and assert the converged balance is correct under the chosen resolution, rather than merely asserting that no error was thrown.
